A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RePO research, with matching authors, central problem, algorithm and theorem. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and Appendices A-D are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original RePO fine-tuning experiments on Alpaca-7B, reward/cost evaluation, GPT-4 comparisons and repeated-seed training curves.

after.justification: V2 reports original experiments on Alpaca-7B and Llama3.2-3B, additional safety-condition analyses, GPT-4 safety assessments and preference-model accuracy results.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the safe/unsafe batch split, clipped surrogate objectives, normalized unsafe objective, capped cumulative penalty and two-critic updates. V2 expands the pseudocode and explicitly includes scaling factors; v1 already documents reward scaling in Appendix C.3. The additional backbone experiments do not establish a new RePO procedure.

E1.justification: V2 adds directly conducted instruction tuning on Alpaca data and preference/safety prediction evaluations for newly trained critic-initialization models (Appendix C.3). V1 used already-trained initial and preference models. Downstream evaluation retains PKU-SafeRLHF, PhysicalSafety, CoNa, Controversial and MaliciousInstructions.

E2.justification: The main quantitative comparator algorithms remain SACPO and PPO-Lagrangian/Beaver, renamed SafeRLHF. V2's Appendix D adds GPT-4o reference responses alongside RePO and the baseline outputs. V1's GPT-4o response appeared only in a separate comparison with Beaver in Appendix A.

E3.justification: V2 adds Llama3.2-3B experiments with SFT, critic fitting and model-specific training settings, plus a separate GPT-4o safety assessment using a score above five. Existing Alpaca comparisons switch from locally trained SACPO to its released checkpoint. Table 1 also changes the stated harmlessness metric from relative cost change to average cost.

E4.justification: The training analysis expands from one initial regime to expected-unsafe, nearly-expected-safe and expected-safe data regimes (v2 Figures 1 and 3), directly testing the proposed safety-compensation mechanism. Appendix D replaces the extensive example gallery with two cross-model cases, removing earlier examples including RePO's unsafe bleach/ammonia response in v1 Table 15.

E5.justification: V1 Figures 1 and 4 and v2 Figure 3 report five independent runs with different seeds and show means and standard deviations. Additional training conditions use the same reporting practice. Neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests for the main benchmark tables.

E6.justification: V2 adds Llama3.2-3B results, including RePO safety rates of 91.46% under model evaluation and 68.60% under GPT-4 evaluation, plus safety-rate breakdowns. Alpaca SACPO's model-based safety entry changes from 75.85% to 80.72% with the checkpoint replacement; RePO's 96.08% is retained. Reported PKU-SafeRLHF GPT-4 win/loss rates against initial Alpaca change from 88%/5% to 82%/10%.

T1.justification: Theorem 1 and its Appendix B proof retain the same rectified min-max equivalence. V2 adds a two-prompt counterexample distinguishing expected from critical safety, formalizes the corresponding policy sets, and discusses Slater's condition and strong duality in Remark 1. No new convergence theorem or algorithmic safety guarantee is established.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains rectified optimization of per-pair safety constraints. V2 narrows the conclusion from best performance in both helpfulness and harmlessness to strongest safety improvement without sacrificing initial-model helpfulness. Renaming safety interference as safety compensation largely preserves the original substantive claim.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the multiplier as a cumulative penalty, revises the explanation for capping it, and connects objective scaling to preventing meaningless high-scoring outputs. It distinguishes low average cost from proximity to critical safety and interprets the SafeRLHF comparison as an ablation. V1's explanation linking SACPO's GPT-4 performance to reduced reward-model overfitting is removed.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds detailed Llama SFT, preference-model and alignment recipes, model access information, and the new safety-evaluation template. It newly specifies Alpaca cost scaling and the PTX coefficient. Reported inference hardware changes from RTX 3080 Ti to RTX 2080 Ti. Conversely, v1's RePO code-access link is absent from v2.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially refocused from a defense-layer taxonomy toward RLHF versus DPO and constrained safety alignment. V2 adds discussion of Huang et al., alignment comparisons by Xu et al. and Li et al., and strong-duality work by Paternain et al., while removing much of the filtering and inference-guidance positioning.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the related work, motivation, method explanation and experimental narrative. The former preliminary pitfalls subsection becomes a standalone section; implementation becomes numbered subsections; experiments are reorganized into setups and results; and the appendix showcase is substantially condensed. Terminology changes throughout.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening example graphic with a policy-set diagram and multipanel diagnostics, replaces circular GPT-4 charts with stacked bars, expands Table 1 across models and evaluators, and expands the scatter plot into six appendix panels. Evaluation templates become tables, and the qualitative tables are replaced and consolidated.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central safety-compensation argument: it tests different initial safety regimes, extends evaluation beyond one backbone, and measures absolute GPT-4 safety rates alongside joint preference judgments. Expanded training recipes and clearer mathematical framing improve assessability. Removing the code link and useful failure examples weakens reproducibility and qualitative transparency, but these losses are outweighed by the more direct and broader empirical testing.
